title: Project Success, Failure, Delays and Abandonment (PMT 801)
subject: Project management
description: Thirty questions across easy, medium and hard on the success criteria, the ten key factors, causes of delay, and project abandonment and collapse.

questions.prompt: Which set gives the four success criteria from Cleland et al (1988)?
options: Time, cost, effectiveness and client's satisfaction
Scope, quality, risk and communication
Design, materials, labour and equipment
Feasibility, viability, appraisal and evaluation
questions.explanation: A project is successful if it passes all four tests.

questions.prompt: What does the effectiveness criterion require?
options: Completion within the approved budget
Completion on the agreed date
Acceptance by the intended users
Completion in accordance with the original performance and quality standards
questions.explanation: Cost is the money criterion, time is the schedule criterion, and acceptance by users is the client's satisfaction criterion.

questions.prompt: What does the client's satisfaction criterion require?
options: Completion in accordance with performance standards
Completion with no cost overrun
Acceptance by the intended users or clients, whether internal or external
Approval by the contractor
questions.explanation: The client or user must accept the final product.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture say about a project that has been physically completed?
options: It is automatically successful
It can still be a failure if it misses the time, cost, quality or client satisfaction criteria
It is a success once the contractor is paid
Physical completion is the only criterion that matters
questions.explanation: The lecture asks about completion date, overruns, quality, durability, realised potential and client and end-user satisfaction.

questions.prompt: How is project abandonment defined?
options: A decision to cancel the idea at the conception phase
Completion of a project ahead of schedule
Handover of a project to a new client
The unplanned suspension of work progress, especially at the execution phase
questions.explanation: Abandonment is mostly seen in the public sector and affects many economic sectors.

questions.prompt: What does project collapse mean in the lecture?
options: A complete death of the project completion process
A temporary pause in work
A change of project team
A revision of the budget
questions.explanation: After a collapse, a new proposal cannot replace the time, cost, quality, material and human resources already used.

questions.prompt: In the ten key factors model, which factor is compared to the brain?
options: Client consultation
Trouble shooting
Communication
Project mission
questions.explanation: Communication coordinates the other factors and receives and transmits signals to them.

questions.prompt: In the ten key factors model, which factor is compared to the heart?
options: Communication
Client consultation
Monitoring and feedback
Personnel
questions.explanation: Without the client there is no project execution, since the client initiates, propels and funds the project.

questions.prompt: How do Aibinu and Jagboro (2002) describe project delays in Nigeria?
options: As endemic
As rare
As limited to private projects
As caused only by bad weather
questions.explanation: They described the growing rate of delays as a major criticism facing the Nigerian construction industry.

questions.prompt: Which measure does the lecture give for mitigating project schedule delays?
options: Fewer site inspections
One-off lump sum funding
Better contract management
Avoiding the use of contractors
questions.explanation: Since much of a project runs through contracts, managing them well is critical.

questions.prompt: Why does looking only at time, cost and performance fail to predict project success?
options: These parameters cannot be measured
It may show immediate contributions to profit, but not whether the project itself was managed correctly
They apply only to completed projects
They ignore profit entirely
questions.explanation: This matters most where an organisation depends on a steady stream of well-managed projects.

questions.prompt: Project success is often measured by the actions of which three groups?
options: The contractor, the supplier and the regulator
The architect, the engineer and the quantity surveyor
The government, the community and the financiers
The project manager and team, the parent organisation, and the customer's organisation
questions.explanation: Each group can take actions that stimulate project success.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the actions the project manager and team can take to stimulate success?
options: Accept team members imposed by the client
Insist on the right to select key project team members
Rely on one type of control tool
Avoid back-up strategies to save cost
questions.explanation: The list also includes avoiding overreliance on one control tool, keeping changes under control and having back-up strategies.

questions.prompt: Which is an action the parent organisation must take, according to the lecture?
options: Pressure the project manager to win contracts
Arbitrarily slash the project team's cost estimate
Encourage buy-ins to win work
Select early a project manager with proven technical, human and administrative skills, in that order
questions.explanation: The other options are things the parent organisation must avoid.

questions.prompt: What must top management do for a project to be successful?
options: Stay out of the project completely
Run all site decisions personally
Recognise it as a project and commit resources and administrative support
Wait for signs of failure before supporting it
questions.explanation: A project cannot be successful unless it is recognised as a project and has top-level support.

questions.prompt: What do the arrows in the ten key factors figure show?
options: All the factors are linked and share responsibility for success, and none can assure success alone
One factor outweighs all the others
Only the client factor matters
The factors act in a fixed sequence
questions.explanation: The model is compared to a functional human body.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture say about choosing project personnel?
options: The client should select all staff
Staff should be selected by tender
The project manager should have full autonomy to recruit people with proven track records, and the client should not impose staff
Track records matter less than cost
questions.explanation: Personnel issues include recruitment, selection and staff training.

questions.prompt: What did the lecture's own model add to the direct factors of time, cost and quality in Morris's model?
options: Materials management factors
Environmental law
Client satisfaction
Contract penalties
questions.explanation: Morris mentioned materials but saw it as a weak point, so the lecture's model incorporated materials management.

questions.prompt: How can too many change orders cause delays, according to Kaliba et al (2008)?
options: They always improve cash flow
They can harm financial performance, which delays the project through shortage of funds
They shorten approval times
They reduce the contractor's workload
questions.explanation: Change orders are one of the possible causes of schedule delays.

questions.prompt: In the survey by Elinwa and Joshua (2001), which party contributed most to time overrun?
options: The contractor, at 62 percent
Others, at 62 percent
The client, at 32 percent
The client, at 62 percent
questions.explanation: Clients, contractors and others contributed 62, 32 and 6 percent respectively.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of party and a cause of delay found by Odeyinka and Yusuf is correct?
options: Client: equipment problems
Contractor: variation orders
Consultant: incomplete drawings and slow response
Weather: slow decision making
questions.explanation: Clients caused delays through variation orders, slow decisions and cash flow problems, and contractors through equipment, planning, finance, materials, inspection and manpower.

questions.prompt: A project authority wants better contract management to reduce delays. Which measure matches the lecture?
options: Insist on realistic and detailed resource and time plans, impose graduated penalties and offer incentives for good performance
Remove penalties so contractors feel supported
Award contracts to the lowest bidder without checking capability
Avoid helping contractors with genuine problems
questions.explanation: The lecture also says contractors should be seen as partners, their competence must be ensured, and authorities should keep the right to off-load contracts early.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture link poor location analysis to project delay?
options: Choosing sites too close to head office
Sites with no assured security, materials or transport that were not analysed at conception can delay the project
Selecting expensive land
Using too many contractors on one site
questions.explanation: Location factors should be properly analysed at the conception phase.

questions.prompt: Why is monitoring and feedback compared to the reproductive organ?
options: It provides the energy that funds the project
It moves the project out of conflicts
It grips the mission of the project
Feedback on each work scope allows work to continue and informs effective planning of the next scope
questions.explanation: The success of each work scope gives feedback to the mission and supports planning of the next scope.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture link procurement delay in public projects to?
options: Bureaucracy, where processing orders can take from weeks to several months
An oversupply of materials
Very fast approval processes
Foreign exchange gains
questions.explanation: The lecture quotes Frimpong et al on the bureaucratic structure of material procurement in developing countries.

questions.prompt: Why is trouble shooting compared to the legs?
options: It coordinates all the other factors
It funds the project like the heart
It defines the aim of the investment
A person must move out to succeed, and the project environment has conflicting issues that must be managed
questions.explanation: Trouble shooting is about managing the conflicts that arise in the project environment.

questions.prompt: Which is a characteristic of project abandonment?
options: The original design always stays valid
The client and team never change
The initial cost and time must change, because inflation, exchange rates and interest rates affect the gap
The project cost stays fixed
questions.explanation: Abandonment may also change the design, the client's taste or the client, the aim of the project and the project team, and may require re-appraisal.

questions.prompt: A project idea is stopped at the conception or planning stage. Does the lecture call this abandonment?
options: Yes, any suspension at any phase is abandonment
No, stopping at conception or planning (initiation) may not be abandonment, which refers to suspension during execution
Yes, but only for public sector projects
Yes, because conception involves a huge financial plan
questions.explanation: Conception to planning is described as initiation.

questions.prompt: Which pair is given as reasons for the abandonment of projects in Nigeria?
options: Excess funds and rapid approvals
Stable government and constant policies
An oversupply of materials and skilled labour
Escalation of cost due to inflation and difficulty paying contractors because of government bureaucracy
questions.explanation: Other reasons include frequent changes in government, increased scope, changes in design and poor project finance arrangements.

questions.prompt: What happens when a building under construction collapses, according to the lecture?
options: It may be impossible to start another structure on the old foundation, and a new proposal needs a completely new network plan
The original network plan can simply resume
The time and cost already spent are recovered
A replacement is quickly built on the same foundation
questions.explanation: A new proposal cannot replace the time, cost, quality, material and human resources already used.
